column5: giving to poor as loan repaid
column6: The commentary joins debt, benefit to another, and eventual recompense; Proverbs calls kindness to the poor a loan to the LORD that he will repay.

column5: rule one's spirit rather than conquer
column6: The commentary's sabır is active self-restraint, and its spear image risks turning truth into force; Proverbs says one slow to anger and ruling his spirit exceeds a mighty city conqueror.
The commentary's vessel rim and stopper picture an inner state kept from spilling out; Proverbs contrasts a fool venting all his spirit with a wise person holding it back.

column5: guard at mouth and door of lips
column6: The commentary compares sabır to the stopper that keeps a vessel's contents from escaping; the psalmist asks the LORD to set a guard over his mouth and watch the door of his lips.
The commentary turns disputed hak into counsel that does not break the neighbor; Proverbs says patience can persuade a ruler and a soft tongue can break bone.

column5: word sustains the weary each morning
column6: The commentary's true advice must hold a companion who weakens and connect one day to the next; the instructed speaker receives a morning-by-morning ear and a word to sustain the weary.

column5: fragile reed spared as justice comes
column6: The commentary's rightful load does not crush one too weak to bear it; the servant does not break a bruised reed or extinguish a faint wick while bringing forth justice faithfully.
The commentary puts endurance after hak because the right must actually arrive; the servant does not grow faint or be crushed until justice is established on earth.

column5: those who spoke become treasured on the day
column6: The commentary's mutual truthful speech survives until each person's due day; after the God-fearers speak together, the LORD promises to make them his treasured possession on the appointed day.
The commentary's final reckoning exposes who actually belongs to the exception; Malachi promises a renewed distinction between righteous and wicked, one serving God and one not.

column5: do work before death ends opportunity
column6: The commentary's finite day gives performed work urgency; Ecclesiastes tells the hearer to do with strength what the hand finds because the grave offers no further work.

The commentary meets day-to-day continuity with patient cultivation; Ecclesiastes says to sow in the morning and not withhold the hand in evening because the grower cannot know which planting will succeed.
The commentary's mutual advice carries a duty to another rather than an optional opinion; Ezekiel is appointed watchman and told to hear God's word and warn Israel on God's behalf.
The commentary's hak is a debt one owes the next person; God says the watchman who fails to warn the wicked shares responsibility for the person's death.

column5: wicked person can turn and live
column6: The commentary says past actions name the rescued group; Ezekiel adds that a formerly wicked person who turns, keeps the statutes, and does justice and righteousness will live, making a changed course decisive.
The commentary calls fasting one form of self-restraint but makes patience an aid to others; Isaiah's chosen fast loosens wicked bonds and lets the oppressed go free.
The commentary's patience remains when an expected harvest and wage do not arrive; Habakkuk names fig, vine, olive, field, flock, and herd all failing.

column5: joy in God despite failed harvest
column6: The commentary's belief provides refuge when work yields loss; after naming failed crops and herds, Habakkuk says he will still rejoice in the LORD who saves.

The commentary holds belief together with lasting right action; this rabbinic reading says Habakkuk reduced the commandments to the single line that the righteous lives by faithfulness, sharpening the role of אמונה in Habakkuk 2:4.

column5: Hillel's reciprocal rule to a convert
column6: The commentary makes advice reciprocal and actionable; Hillel tells the prospective convert not to do to another what is hateful to himself and then sends him to study the rest.

column5: disputes for heaven and disputes for self
column6: The commentary contrasts contending over hak with handing it on; the mishnah distinguishes disputes for Heaven, exemplified by Hillel and Shammai, from Korah's self-seeking dispute, so disagreement itself is not condemned.

column5: strive for truth under mortal threat
column6: The commentary couples defending the true word with patience when speaking costs something; Sirach urges fighting for truth even to death and promises God's support.

column5: faithful friend as medicine of life
column6: The commentary's bitter remedy and another person's sustaining patience meet in a single image; Sirach calls a faithful friend a medicine of life.

The commentary defines sabır as holding oneself in place rather than rushing away; a parent-like instructor tells the learner to set the heart right, remain steadfast, and not become hasty in trouble.
The commentary puts patience after an acted and spoken right that may bring hardship; Sirach tells the hearer to accept what comes and be patient through humiliating reversals.

column5: dying father enjoins children to uphold covenant
column6: The commentary's will joins generations through an actionable word; Mattathias charges his children at death to be zealous for the law and give their lives for the ancestral covenant.

column5: work of faith, labor of love, steadfast hope
column6: The commentary orders belief, good work, and patience as defining actions; Paul remembers the community's work of faith, labor of love, and steadfastness of hope together.

column5: faith grows and mutual love increases
column6: The commentary moves from individual belief to reciprocal support; Paul thanks God that the congregation's faith grows and the love of every member for one another increases.
The commentary says the truth people share may have a cost they must help one another bear; Paul boasts of the community's endurance and faith amid persecutions and afflictions.
The commentary refuses to leave iman at mere inward assent; Paul says what counts is faith working through love, directly joining belief with outward relation.
The commentary's joined plants give food through lasting good action; Paul calls love, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, and faithfulness fruit of the Spirit.
The commentary joins purposeful deeds to a true word passed among people; the letter calls children to love in deed and truth, rather than word or speech alone.
The commentary pairs belief with reciprocal action; this command says to believe in the Son's name and love one another, turning faith into a shared duty.

The commentary's hak includes a neighbor's concrete due and its sabır sustains the weak; the letter asks how divine love remains in one who sees a sibling in need yet closes the heart while possessing worldly goods.
The commentary's inherited advice should become a walked path; the elder rejoices that some of the addressee's children are walking in truth as commanded by the Father.

column5: love one another as inherited command
column6: The commentary's will is a binding word passed onward; the elder asks the addressee to love one another, calling it a command held from the beginning.
The commentary says a recommended truth must be worked into conduct; the letter defines love by walking according to the commandments already heard.
The commentary's sound work does not disappear when the day's capital runs out; Hebrews says God will not overlook the work and love shown through service to fellow believers.
The commentary grounds endurance in a due promise; Hebrews tells the community to imitate those who inherit promises through faith and patience.

column5: flee to refuge and hold hope
column6: The commentary hears both safety and active holding in iman and sabır; Hebrews describes people who have fled for refuge and grasp the hope set before them.
The commentary's vessel stopper and firm rock picture an inner good held against a storm; Hebrews calls hope a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul.
The commentary's reliable road and intentional work require persistence; Hebrews calls believers to lay aside encumbrance and run their appointed race with endurance.

column5: Jesus endures cross for future joy
column6: The commentary says a trustworthy outcome makes painful patience meaningful; Hebrews presents Jesus enduring the cross for the joy set before him.
The commentary gives true counsel and patience their own places; Paul orders preaching, reproof, rebuke, and exhortation with all patience and teaching.
The commentary's believer pursues sound conduct and patience together; Paul commands pursuit of righteousness, faith, love, endurance, and gentleness.
The commentary distinguishes believing from holding another through hardship; Titus is to teach older men to be sound in faith, love, and endurance.
The commentary binds taking refuge in trust to active good work under suffering; Peter tells those suffering according to God's will to entrust their souls to a faithful creator while doing good.

column5: do good and endure unjust suffering
column6: The commentary's patient truth costs its speaker something; Peter says enduring suffering incurred for doing good is pleasing to God.
The commentary opposes quarrelling over truth to giving truthful counsel; Peter commands a ready account of hope to questioners, delivered with gentleness and respect.

column5: walk worthily and bear fruit in good work
column6: The commentary joins road, useful vegetation, and sound action; Paul prays that believers walk worthy of the Lord while bearing fruit in every good work.
The commentary says the group must hold its place under pressure; Paul asks that believers receive power for all endurance and patience with joy.

column5: hope, endurance in trouble, steady prayer
column6: The commentary's patient waiting is active and grounded in a promised good; Paul calls believers to rejoice in hope, endure affliction, and persevere in prayer.
The commentary's final day gives every person the due of their work; Paul states that God will repay each person according to works.

column5: all appear for deeds to be recompensed
column6: The commentary's Hāqqa confronts each worker with what was done; Paul says all must appear before Christ's judgment seat to receive what is due for bodily deeds, good or bad.
The commentary specifically meets vegetation with intentional construction; Paul calls the community God's field and God's building in a single verse.

column5: work survives and worker receives wage
column6: The commentary measures the soundness of a worker's deed by whether it lasts through the final day; Paul says the builder whose work survives the fire receives a reward.
The commentary relates escape from loss to good work that remains; Paul allows a different outcome in which a person's work burns and brings loss while the person is saved through fire.
The commentary's securely fitted work is proved by pressure rather than appearance; Jesus' rock-founded house survives rain, floods, and winds because its foundation holds.
The commentary's joined green growth needs patient holding after belief; Jesus says the rocky-ground hearers believe for a while but fall away in a time of testing because they lack root.
The commentary turns disputed hak into counsel that repairs and yields sound deeds; James calls heavenly wisdom peaceable, gentle, merciful, and full of good fruits.
The commentary's linked vegetation and reconciliation are carried by patience; James says a harvest of righteousness is sown in peace by those making peace.
The commentary says speaking truth may bring the hardship for which patient support is needed; James offers the prophets who spoke in the Lord's name as examples of suffering and patience.
The commentary's reciprocal true advice reconnects a person who has broken from the path; James tells the community that someone can bring back a member wandering from the truth.
The commentary's saving exception is sustained by one person's intervention for another; James says turning a sinner from wandering saves a soul from death and covers sins.
The commentary's sabır must hold through the whole threatened period; Jesus says the one who endures to the end will be saved.
The commentary orders faith, sound obedience, and patience as traits of those rescued; Revelation calls for the saints' endurance, identifying them as command-keepers who hold faith in Jesus.
The commentary's threatened believers ask for patience up to death; the risen speaker tells the persecuted assembly to be faithful unto death and promises the crown of life.
The commentary makes inherited teaching and communal belonging mutually necessary; the first believers devote themselves to apostolic teaching and fellowship, shared meals, and prayer.
The commentary's right includes a share owed to someone lacking support; the believers distribute sale proceeds according to each person's need.

The commentary's individual believers become a connected group in which each can sustain another; Acts describes the multitude of believers as one heart and soul and not claiming possessions as purely private.
The commentary's joined pasture leaves no hungry gap between members; Acts says none of the believers was needy because owners sold property for distribution.

column5: do good and lend even to enemies
column6: The commentary's hak includes a debt owed and sabır that can transform an enemy; Jesus commands doing good and lending without expecting return to enemies, and promises a great reward.

column5: bless, pray, and fast for persecutors
column6: The commentary's patient answer turns hostility into a healing bond and includes fasting as restraint; the Didache urges blessing cursers, praying for enemies, and fasting for persecutors.

column5: strong support weak; rich help poor
column6: The commentary's community takes another's weight when that person cannot stand; Clement says the strong should care for the weak and the rich provide for the poor.

column5: Arabic ء م ن / Hebrew אמנ; table sound correspondence
column6: The commentary's advice links generations to something enduring; the psalm joins God's faithfulness, אמונה, through all generations to the firm establishment of the earth.

column5: Arabic ء م ن / Hebrew אמנ; table sound correspondence
column6: The commentary combines trust and a walked right path; the psalmist chooses the way of faithfulness, אמונה, and sets God's judgments before himself.
The commentary contrasts capital that shrinks with good action that lasts; the righteous person distributes to the poor and his righteousness endures forever.
The commentary defines patience as keeping still without losing confidence; Isaiah says salvation lies in returning and rest, strength in quietness and trust, while the addressees refuse.

column5: right instruction in heart without fear
column6: The commentary makes belief a refuge for bearers of true speech; God addresses people with his law in their hearts and tells them not to fear human reproach.
The commentary makes advice an act owed to another, not control over their response; the watchman who warns the wicked has saved his own life even if the wicked refuses to turn.

The commentary says completed actions characterize those excepted from loss; Ezekiel insists that someone once righteous can turn to injustice and die in it, preserving moral reversal beyond a fixed label.
The commentary connects paying another's due to an unmeasured return; Moses says to give a poor brother generously and without a begrudging heart, promising blessing in the giver's work.
The commentary's sabır can mean standing guarantor for another's debt; Proverbs warns that pledging oneself for a stranger brings suffering, providing a limit to that secondary image.
The commentary defines patience as restraining the inner cry under an inescapable blow; Job rebukes his wife for accepting good but rejecting adversity from God and does not sin with his lips.

column5: wait quietly for the day of trouble
column6: The commentary's patience remains still before a promised day even with bodily alarm; Habakkuk trembles at the vision yet resolves to wait quietly for the day of distress.
The commentary's dependable load animal and mountain stand for not stumbling under pressure; Habakkuk calls God his strength and says he makes his feet like a deer's on the heights.
The commentary joins iman to a road that can be walked patiently; Sirach directs the son to trust God for help and make his ways straight.

column5: guarantor gives his life for another
column6: The commentary develops sabır as a friend who underwrites someone else's debt; Sirach tells the debtor not to forget the guarantor's kindness because that person has put life at risk for him.
The commentary says belief and work can be individual but saving advice must pass between people; Hillel asks what a person is if only for himself.

column5: world stands on teaching and kindness
column6: The commentary's sound community combines a true word with useful action; the mishnah names Torah, worship, and acts of lovingkindness as supports on which the world stands.

column5: legal right alone does not repair society
column6: The commentary moves hak from winning a dispute toward mutually owed care; the Talmud says Jerusalem's downfall was connected to judging by strict law without going beyond its letter.
The commentary says speaking right may bring hostile blows and demand patience; the opponents in Wisdom propose insult and torture to test the righteous person's gentleness and endurance.
The commentary's bitter medicine and earned due meet in suffering that proves worth; Wisdom says the righteous, disciplined for a little while, receive great good after God tests them.
The commentary moves from believing to work of a specified quality; Peter asks believers to supplement faith with virtue rather than leave faith unworked.
The commentary defines sabır as first holding oneself, then remaining in place; Peter's sequence moves from knowledge to self-control and from self-control to endurance.
The commentary's self-restraint becomes a bond with the next person; Peter's sequence leads from endurance to godliness, sibling affection, and love.
The commentary's patient person remains held under a blow; Paul describes believers as persecuted yet not abandoned and struck down yet not destroyed.
The commentary joins the passing day with an inner good kept from loss; Paul says that even as the outer person wastes away the inner person is renewed day by day.

column5: brief suffering and weight of glory
column6: The commentary's right load, labor, and reward meet in a paradox; Paul says momentary affliction prepares an eternal weight of glory beyond comparison.
The commentary contrasts passing worldly capital with something that remains; Paul directs attention from seen temporary things to unseen eternal ones.
The commentary says patient action must hold to the end of the day; Hebrews asks each hearer to show the same diligence for full assurance of hope until the end.

column5: faith as assurance of hoped reality
column6: The commentary hears trust in the truth of a promise before it arrives; Hebrews defines faith by confidence concerning what is hoped for and conviction about what is not seen.
The commentary binds an advised truth to practiced action and endurance; Paul reminds Timothy that he observed Paul's teaching, conduct, purpose, faith, patience, love, and steadfastness.
The commentary makes repeated work over time a defining completed act; Paul says he fought the good fight, finished the race, and kept the faith.

column5: righteous crown due on the day
column6: The commentary's finished work and patient wait meet a day of due recompense; Paul says the righteous judge will award him the crown on that day.
The commentary's true word can become a defended standard under mortal threat; the faithful conquer by their testimony and do not cling to life even when facing death.
The commentary's patience keeps connected people from splitting apart; Jesus says increasing lawlessness makes the love of many grow cold before his call to endure.
The commentary tests whether a sound deed nourishes the next person; the king names feeding, giving drink, and welcoming as acts that mark those accepted at judgment.

column5: care for least counted as service
column6: The commentary's mutual support gives a needy neighbor a concrete claim; the king identifies deeds done for the least of his brothers with deeds done for him.

column5: believers gather with things in common
column6: The commentary's scattered patches become a joined group; Acts says believers stay together and hold their possessions in common before describing need-based distribution.
The commentary's shared hak is an actual material due; believers lay sale proceeds at the apostles' feet and distribution is made according to need.

column5: life lost for true message is saved
column6: The commentary's rescue from loss can require holding fast under threat; Jesus says one who loses life for him and the gospel will save it.
The commentary contrasts handing on hak with pulling it into a dispute; Paul describes the self-seeking as disobedient to truth and obedient to injustice.
The commentary contrasts capital that distracts with useful fruit that lasts; Jesus says life's cares, riches, and pleasures choke the heard word so its hearers fail to mature fruit.

The commentary's guarantor carries another's weakness and its worker anticipates gain; Ignatius urges Polycarp to bear everyone's infirmities like a trained athlete and links harder labor to greater gain.
The commentary's hard stone and straight blow make patience a strength under impact; Ignatius compares the addressed leader to an anvil that receives strikes and stays firm.
The commentary's day of work comes to its wage; Clement contrasts the diligent worker who can receive bread from the employer with the idle one who cannot face him.

column5: shared funds sustain people in need
column6: The commentary's reciprocal counsel must become practical provision; Justin describes a gathered Christian community collecting voluntary gifts for orphans, widows, the sick, strangers, and prisoners.
The commentary's linked pasture feeds people unable to sustain themselves; Tertullian describes voluntary community contributions used for the poor, bereaved, aged, shipwrecked, and imprisoned.

column5: world as antechamber for coming world
column6: The commentary's brief working day prepares an enduring recompense; this saying makes the present world a vestibule in which a person prepares for the next, though its architectural image only indirectly meets the commentary's work-and-wage scene.

column5: patience rules anger and supports right acts
column6: The commentary's sabır restrains the inner eruption before it harms others; Hermas contrasts patience with anger and connects patience with righteous conduct, though subsection numbering varies among editions.
